evidence: binding_lifecycle.py retire() docstring: 'RETIRED FIRST, live second ... the entry must be durable in the retired file BEFORE the live binding is dropped, or a crash between the two would lose it from both ... That order is a contract, not an implementation detail'
retire() body: self._repo.save_retired(retired_entries) ... then self._bindings.pop(local_id, None); self._reverse.pop(jira_key, None); self._repo.save()
search_files over tests/unit/rebar_reconciler/state/test_binding_lifecycle.py for 'save_retired': only a fixture setup hit at line 983, no ordering/fault-injection test
search_files over the named facade regression suite test_binding_absence_lifecycle.py for 'save_retired' and 'order': (no matches) — the contract is not covered there either

ABSENCE: a test that monkeypatches the live save() (or save_retired) to raise, then asserts the retired file already holds the tombstone (retired-durable-before-live-drop) would fail if the order were reversed; no such test exists
dropped.finding: The 'RETIRED FIRST, live second' durability ordering, which retire()'s docstring explicitly calls 'a contract, not an implementation detail' (a crash between save_retired and dropping the live binding must not lose the entry from both files), has no test that injects a fault between the two writes to prove the ordering holds. Existing tests only assert the post-retirement end state, which a wrong write order (live-first) would still satisfy on a clean run.
scenarios: A mechanical refactor reorders retire() to drop the live binding before writing the retired file; every existing test still passes because they only check the final steady state, but a real mid-operation crash now loses the binding from both files.
